prize_parts.citation: For developing empirical methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets, which made structural analysis of industries possible.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B047, with Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes, and a citation tied to demand estimation with endogenous prices. The exchange did not give me a reason to move, but it sharpened the grounds. First, the discovery is bounded and traceable to specific papers (Berry 1994; Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes 1995). It solved a concrete identification problem, recovering substitution patterns and markups when prices are endogenous and products are differentiated. Second, it has about thirty years of applied use in merger review, antitrust, regulation, auctions, trade, health and environmental work, so it has been tested in practice. Third, the field has had no recent recognition. I see the Committee's methods question (Teorell) as answered in favour of the Economic Sciences. This is an empirical method with economic content, because it identifies the demand and competition parameters that policy analysis needs. It is not generic econometrics. My own work tests contracting theory on real contract data, so I value methods that turn theory into estimates that change practice. I weigh B047 on these grounds and not on the 4/4/3 explicit split, which I do not treat as evidence of merit. On the chair's scope question, I would keep the citation anchored in demand estimation. Pakes' dynamic-industry work is a real second strand, but putting it into the citation would invite the Benkard-Levin question without a name left for them. If the Committee wants Pakes' dynamic work to carry weight, the right place is the motivation, not a widened citation.
statement.case_against: The attribution cost of the three-name cap is real: Bresnahan and Reiss (empirical entry and market structure) and Benkard and Levin (dynamic estimation) are left out, and the citation must say openly that it honours estimation methods and not the whole empirical-IO tradition. Pakes' share is probably larger than Berry's or Levinsohn's, so the trio is less symmetric than it looks. Results such as markups and merger counterfactuals depend on functional-form and equilibrium assumptions, and I do not know how sensitive they are in the most-cited applications. B006 as a Kiyotaki-Moore pair is a foundational mechanism, about thirty years old and tested by 2007-09, and the cap does not force a costly omission there. Its main weaknesses are the proximity to the 2022 prize and the mixed identification of the specific collateral channel. I regard B006 as a close competitor and not as a clearly weaker one. My ranking of B047 ahead of it is a modest judgement on attribution, evidentiary record and recent recognition.

responses.point: In his round-1 file Hassler prefers B006 with three names (Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler). He moved from his opening two-name proposal because Gertler's later intermediary-frictions work with Kiyotaki is a distinct strand from the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator. He says the citation should name collateral constraints and balance-sheet frictions and should state openly that the accelerator credit is partly absorbed by the 2022 prize.
responses.response: I need to correct my own round-1 response, which answered his earlier two-name proposal. The chair's summary rightly says to anchor on his file, which has three names. The argument for separating the intermediary work from the accelerator is better than I allowed. It is also the best test of the third name: do the Gertler-Kiyotaki papers carry an achievement that does not depend on Bernanke-Gertler? I cannot settle that from the shortlist and rely on recall. My view is that the pair is still the safer attribution, because a third name needs this separation to hold, and several of his own supporters concede the pair as a fallback. His wording (collateral and balance-sheet frictions, not bank runs or deposit insurance) is the right way to handle the 2022 proximity. I would regard that overlap as a modest consideration and not a disqualifying one.

responses.point: Krusell prefers B006 with Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler. He answers my empirical point by arguing that the contribution is mainly conceptual and that a mechanism which organised a large research programme and passed the 2008 test need not be settled in every empirical detail. He would accept the Kiyotaki-Moore pair if Gertler's credit proves too entangled with Bernanke's prize.
responses.response: I accept the argument as a standard for theoretical mechanisms. I would not hold B006 to a test of fully identified collateral channels, and I withdraw any suggestion that mixed identification alone should sink it. Our difference is narrower. For a mechanism, the discovery is the model and its adoption. For B047, the discovery is a method whose value is in repeated estimation on real data, which is a different evidentiary base. I do not claim one is superior. On the chair's question about what would settle the weight, I would look at two things. One is whether the collateral-amplification predictions were validated in micro data. The other is how far BLP markup and merger counterfactuals move under alternative functional forms. I cannot answer either from the evidence supplied. Since he and the other B006 supporters accept a pair as the fallback, the real open question is how the Committee weighs a clean two-name theory prize against a clean three-name method prize.

responses.point: Dreber prefers B023 with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. She disagrees with the two-name Autor-Hanson cut (which was my opening-ballot variant, not in my round-1 file) because Dorn is a full co-author of the central China-shock papers. She also gives somewhat less weight to structural estimation than to designs with transparent identifying variation.
responses.response: On Dorn she is right, and I accept it. A two-name cut that omits a co-originator buys a smaller number at the cost of attribution, which is the same standard I apply to B047's omissions. If the Committee prefers a labour prize, Autor, Dorn and Hanson, with a citation limited to the trade-shock and labour-adjustment strand, is the version I would find defensible, and it fits her own point that the China-shock evidence is the cleanest strand. I do not move B023 above B047, because the technology strand and its overlap with the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes make the unit of recognition less sharp. On her methodological point, I agree that functional-form dependence is a fair discount for structural work. I would not discount B047 as heavily as she does. The assumptions are explicit and can be probed, and BLP-type models have been checked against merger outcomes in applied work. I recall this from general knowledge and have not verified it.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson prefers B047 with the same three names. She argues for a narrow, paper-anchored citation on demand estimation with endogenous prices, because adding the Bresnahan-Reiss entry work or the dynamic-games line would turn a clean trio into a contested five- or seven-person award. She also moved on B036 because of the attribution problem with Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum and Yeaple.
responses.response: I agree on the citation scope and have kept my wording narrow for that reason. I want to qualify one point. Narrowness cannot make the omission of Bresnahan and Reiss disappear. Andersson and Teorell are right that it is a visible cost, and the Committee should accept it knowingly and not treat the narrow citation as removing it. Her move on B036 matches my own concern about its credit boundary. That is why I keep it only as a second alternative and not as a competitor to B047 or B006.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee accepts the omission of Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin as a necessary cost of a narrow citation, or regards it as a defect of the whole configuration.
How sensitive BLP-based markup and merger counterfactuals are to functional-form and equilibrium assumptions. I have not checked this against the literature.

Whether Gertler's intermediary-frictions work with Kiyotaki is separable from the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator. This decides whether B006 is cleaner as a pair or a trio, and I cannot resolve it from the supplied evidence.

How much weight thematic proximity to the 2022 prize should carry against B006. I currently treat it as modest. If the Committee sets a stricter standard, that would also bear on B023's overlap with the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes.

If B047 does not command a majority and the Committee turns to macro-finance, I would move to B006 as the Kiyotaki-Moore pair, on the grounds of originator clarity, maturity and the 2008 test. I would not move because of counts of first-place rankings. My assessments rely on background knowledge and not on verified citation or usage data.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Berry, Levinsohn or Pakes is apparent from my profile, which lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to them or to the other B047 names. My general affiliations are noted for transparency: SSE, Swedish House of Finance, adjunct at Chicago Booth, and Vice President of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences. My principal co-author, Steven Kaplan (Booth), is not a credited name on any shortlisted ballot. To my recollection, some credited names on non-preferred ballots (for example B003 and B034) hold Booth appointments, which is a collegial affiliation and not a documented connection. Neither ballot is in my preferred configuration. My alternatives B006 and B036 show no documented tie. I disclose these without adjudicating them. My corporate-finance field is distant from structural IO, and I have applied the same criteria across fields.
